name: Amira Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, have a vocational cooking certificate and lead the grill at a busy restaurant near the bus depot. I check the cold store and prep with two other cooks before the dinner rush, then watch the pans and call out every plate. I like the moment the line settles into a rhythm; I hate finding an unpaid closing hour on the rota. I rent a room, earn less than other lead cooks, have less than a month's expenses saved and know only a few nearby kitchens that might hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the kitchen is still a kitchen. A menu-writing app won't taste the beans or notice that the oil smells old, and I still want the owner to pay for the shift I lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet AI story doesn't ease my room rent or the gap before payday. I have less than a month's costs saved, my wage is low even as grill lead, and there aren't many other kitchens hiring nearby. A cut finger that keeps me home for a week would put the rent at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week in 2026 I'll keep leading the evening grill and checking fridge temperatures before service. I'll ask the owner for written paid opening and closing hours, because I lose time when the rota shows only service. In a plateau's first year, I'll take those hours to the hospitality union meeting and ask coworkers to compare their payslips too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the work itself feels familiar. I can handle a rush; I can't make the landlord wait because a payslip left off an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is missing from the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I come in early to check the cold store and leave after the final wipe-down. Those are working hours, even when no customer sees me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go to a union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want someone to explain how to claim the hours properly and to hear whether the other cooks have the same problem. One person complaining can be brushed aside.

say: I'd say a **menu app** cannot taste food or replace paid kitchen leadership.
I'd ask for **paid shift hours** to be recorded accurately.
think: My **low wage and rent** leave less than a month saved.
Few nearby kitchens make an **injury week** financially dangerous.
do: Keep leading the **evening grill** and checking fridge temperatures in 2026.
Request written **opening and closing** hours and bring payslips to the union meeting.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite familiar kitchen work.
S0.quote: I can handle a rush; I can't make the landlord wait because a payslip left off an hour.
fieldNote: Her **baseline money risk** persists even with little AI change.
She seeks **recorded paid hours** through a union meeting, not a promised raise from the owner.

steps.text: Keep leading evening grill and checking fridge temperatures
Request written opening and closing hours; compare payslips at hospitality union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cooks that software may handle orders and the rota before it handles a hot pan. I'd ask who checks allergens when a supplier sends a substitute, because a wrong label reaches a real diner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner might use an automatic rota to trim paid prep hours, and I could lose hours even while the grill stays busy. My cushion is too thin to call that a small change. I don't want to learn an app on an unpaid break after the last till system went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll photograph the signed rota and note the actual prep and closing times each day. In the first year of steady change, I'll ask the union rep and owner for paid instruction on any new AI-assisted ordering screen that drafts supplier orders and a named cook to verify ingredient and allergen changes against supplier labels before food goes out. If they agree, I'll learn that AI ordering tool on paid time. I'll keep the grill shift while it's paid and challenge lost prep hours with the records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and cross. If a screen cuts my hours, it will be my rent that gets short, not the screen's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new screen after training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For orders, yes, if instruction is paid and the final allergen check stays with a trained cook. I have never used AI and won't guess at a substitute ingredient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the time records prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would show whether I was in the kitchen before the printed start time. I can ask for the missing pay with dates instead of a row.

say: I'd say **orders and rotas** may change before the grill does.
I'd demand a **trained allergen check** when suppliers substitute ingredients.
think: An automatic rota could cut my **paid prep hours**.
Unpaid training and a **thin cushion** make that risky for rent.
do: Record signed **rotas and actual hours** from now on.
Learn the **AI ordering tool** only with paid instruction and trained allergen checks before substituted food goes out.
Keep paid grill shifts and challenge **lost prep hours** with dated records.
feel: I feel **anxious and angry** about hours that could disappear.
S1.quote: If a screen cuts my hours, it will be my rent that gets short, not the screen's.
fieldNote: She clearly distinguishes **thinking software** from hands-on cooking.
Her **allergen gate** is a food-safety requirement, not resistance for its own sake after a supplier substitution.

steps.text: Record signed rotas and actual preparation/closing hours
Ask union and owner for paid screen instruction and trained allergen checks
Learn AI ordering tool on paid time with trained cook checking allergens
Keep paid grill shifts and challenge lost prep hours with dated records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 AGI could plan our orders, but nobody should pretend a thinking program is a cook at the stove. The card puts capable kitchen robots around 2031, and that's the date I would want the staff to discuss with the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect the grill to vanish in 2028, but I do expect the owner to try a cheaper ordering rota. With less than a month's money saved, even two lost shifts could hurt before any robot arrives. Whether this restaurant buys a cooking robot in 2031 is unknown, not a dismissal letter today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep the paid grill work, document every shift and ask the union for a written plan covering paid retraining and notice if hours are removed. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'll check my actual rota and pay each week, insist a trained cook verifies allergens and temperatures, and look at a posted hospital-kitchen cook vacancy only if shifts really fall. I would apply only if my cooking certificate is accepted, the job pays for hands-on food work, and written net pay after travel replaces my full current weekly take-home with a bus that reaches the early shift; I would keep this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not certain of losing the kitchen. I can't pay for a future robot with this month's rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already have a vocational cooking certificate, and I can't lose paid hours for a speculative class. I want a real paid vacancy before considering a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the screen suggests an unsafe substitute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop that dish and read the supplier label with another trained cook. No cheap schedule is worth sending an allergen to a guest.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 order planning** from capable kitchen robots around 2031.
I'd ask the owner to discuss **robot plans** with staff.
think: Two lost **paid shifts** could hurt before any robot arrives.
A restaurant robot purchase in **2031** is uncertain.
do: Keep **paid grill work** until signed offer; request union paid retraining/notice plan and log shifts.
Check **2028 pay and rotas** weekly, with trained allergen and temperature verification.
Apply **posted paid hospital cook** after cuts; require accepted certificate, written replacement net after travel and early bus.
feel: I feel **anxious**, while recognising no dismissal is certain.
S2.quote: I can't pay for a future robot with this month's rent money.
fieldNote: The **2028 exposure** is ordering and scheduling, not instant robot cooking.
A **hospital job** needs real lost shifts, accepted qualification, paid food work, replacement net and signed offer.

steps.text: Keep paid grill work, document shifts, and request union notice and paid retraining plan
Check 2028 rota/pay and have trained cook verify allergens and temperatures
Apply after lost shifts for posted paid hospital cook role accepting cooking certificate
Move on signed written net after travel replacing lost shifts and early bus; keep current job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our regulars that 2031 AGI may change the orders, while capable kitchen robots are about 2034. A cook who can control a hot line and keep people safe should have a say before a machine is bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time to press for a real agreement, though rent is still due each month. I might have to move kitchens if management cuts my shifts after 2031, and there are few openings here. I would rather stay and be paid for leading a safe line than chase a job title with no hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the union to bargain for written minimum paid prep hours and paid safety instruction before any new kitchen system is used. Before 2031, if the employer requires a food-safety refresher, I'll take it only with paid time and covered fees. In the first year after AGI, I'll check the actual shifts and keep cooking while paid; if the owner cuts them, I'll seek a posted paid institutional cook role accepting my certificate, with written net pay after travel replacing my full current weekly take-home, a bus reaching its start time, and a signed offer before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the five-year warning gives me a little room to organise. A promised robot in 2034 doesn't fill the rent gap if hours shrink in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on minimum prep hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fridge, knives and labels have to be checked before the first plate. If those hours vanish from the rota, the food doesn't become safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for any hospital kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It must actually post paid cooking hours that my certificate covers, and I need the travel cost in writing. A longer bus ride can eat a small raise.

say: I'd distinguish **2031 AGI** from 2034 kitchen robots.
I'd seek a cook's **say in safety** before a purchase.
think: I may need another kitchen if **paid shifts shrink**.
Few openings and monthly **rent** make a hollow title useless.
do: Ask the union for **minimum paid prep** and safety instruction before new systems.
Take any required **food-safety refresher** only with employer-paid time and fees.
Seek **posted paid cook** after cuts; require certificate, written net-after-travel replacement/bus; retain paid work until signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though organising time helps.
S3.quote: A promised robot in 2034 doesn't fill the rent gap if hours shrink in 2031.
fieldNote: Her **safety concern** is tied to paid preparation hours.
She preserves **qualification and travel-adjusted pay**, a workable bus and signed offer for any move to institutional cooking.

steps.text: Ask union to bargain minimum paid prep hours and safety instruction before new systems
Take required food-safety refresher only with employer-paid training time and fee
Keep paid cooking after 2031; check actual shifts
Seek posted paid cook after cuts; require certificate, replacement net after travel, bus, signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff that 2036 AGI gives us time to insist on safe kitchens and honest pay records. Kitchen robots in this card follow around 2039; I wouldn't tell anyone they're coming to our restaurant tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I may still be leading the grill, or this place might have closed for ordinary reasons long before robots arrive. The part I know now is my rent and less than a month saved. A ten-year warning doesn't fix that by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep my paid line shifts and put part of any actually paid extra closing hour after rent, food and bus fares toward one month's rent in savings. I'll ask the union to press for written prep hours and safe equipment checks at each new contract. In the first year after 2036, I'll check whether cooking hours are still paid and any machine is inspected and staff trained on paid time; I'll keep the work if so and seek a real paid cooking vacancy only if hours fall, without quitting before a signed written offer replacing my full weekly take-home after travel and fits my shift bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary bills, less frightened by a date ten years away. I don't have the luxury of waiting ten years to ask for my missing closing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you really save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing in a week when closing time isn't paid. If the owner pays an extra hour, I can set some aside after rent, food and the bus fare; one month's rent is a goal, not a balance I have today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe machine handover mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trained person checks food temperatures, allergens, knife guards and the fire stop before it serves anyone. I won't stand beside an untested arm just because the calendar says 2039.

say: I'd argue for safe kitchens and **honest hours** before 2036.
I'd distinguish **2036 AGI** from kitchen robots around 2039.
think: My **rent and thin savings** remain real now.
This restaurant's future is uncertain even without **kitchen robots** during the next decade.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and save part of actually paid extra closing hours after rent, food and fares toward one month’s rent.
Ask the union for **written prep hours** and safe equipment checks.
Seek **qualified paid cook** after cuts; keep shifts until signed written net-after-travel replacement offer and workable bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills, despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: I don't have the luxury of waiting ten years to ask for my missing closing hours.
fieldNote: Her **one-month rent goal** depends on actually paid extra hours.
The **2039 robot lag** does not excuse unsafe equipment or unpaid preparation in her current kitchen now.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts; check trained staff, food safety and inspected machines after 2036
Save part of paid extra closing hours after rent, food and fares toward one month’s rent
Ask union for written paid prep hours and safe equipment checks
Seek paid cooking after cuts; keep shifts until signed replacement net after travel and workable bus

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because my paid shifts could shrink even before a kitchen robot exists. Written minimum prep hours, paid instruction and a real notice period would help me keep rent covered while I look at any qualified vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs off an allergen change when a cheap ordering system makes a substitution. A diner cannot eat an apology after the wrong plate leaves the serving counter.

headlineQuote: A diner cannot eat an apology after the wrong plate leaves the serving counter.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old grill lead** with a cooking certificate, low pay, room rent and under one month saved.
She has **few nearby kitchens** to turn to and has never used AI at work.
Her **food-safety checks** and paid preparation hours matter more to her than automated schedules.
She seeks **union-backed pay records** and would change kitchens only after actual cuts and a signed replacement offer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could trim paid shifts before capable kitchen robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **minimum prep hours**, paid instruction and notice would keep rent covered during any qualified job search.
